about: What a terrestrial analog cannot reproduce. Shown next to every candidate, never mixed into the similarity score.
status: Reference values; check each number against its source before quoting it in the submission.

sources.fact_sheets: NASA Planetary Fact Sheets (Earth, Moon, Mars), NSSDCA
sources.mars_radiation: Hassler, D. M., et al. (2014). Mars' surface radiation environment measured with the Mars Science Laboratory's Curiosity rover. Science, 343, 1244797.
sources.moon_radiation: Zhang, S., et al. (2020). First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface. Science Advances, 6, eaaz1334.
sources.earth_radiation: UNSCEAR 2008 Report: world average natural background dose.

quantities.name: Surface gravity
quantities.workaround: Parabolic flights, suspension rigs, scaled mass models.

quantities.name: Surface pressure
quantities.note: Mars varies with season between about 400 and 870 Pa; the Moon is a hard vacuum.

quantities.name: Length of the solar day
quantities.note: The lunar day lasts 29.53 Earth days: about two weeks of light and two weeks of darkness away from the poles.
quantities.workaround: Simulated schedules; polar day and night at high latitudes for long light or darkness.

quantities.name: Tilt of the spin axis
quantities.note: Moon: tilt to the ecliptic. It is why the polar Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon.
quantities.workaround: High-latitude sites in the season of low Sun (see the low-Sun layer).

quantities.name: Sunlight above the atmosphere
quantities.workaround: Scale by the ratio; no atmosphere on the Moon means harsher light and darker shadows.

quantities.name: Radiation dose equivalent on the surface
quantities.note: Earth: 2.4 mSv per year of natural background. Galactic cosmic rays only; solar particle events add more.

quantities.name: Surface temperature
quantities.note: Lunar cold traps: Diviner measurements in permanently shadowed craters. Compute the values of each target from the Diviner PRP file instead of quoting these.
quantities.workaround: Antarctic and Arctic sites for cold; thermal-vacuum chambers for cryogenic cases.
